explanation: In 1889 an agent of Thomas Edison recorded Brahms in Vienna playing part of his Hungarian Dance No. 1 on a wax cylinder. The sound is faint and very crackly.

claims.text: A recording of Johannes Brahms playing the piano exists.
Theo Wangemann, working for Thomas Edison, recorded Brahms in Vienna in 1889.
On the recording Brahms plays part of his Hungarian Dance No. 1.
The Brahms recording was made on a wax cylinder and is very noisy.

Claims: every checkable statement in the stem, options and explanation is listed, with risk at or above the C26 floor and raised where a fact is beyond everyday knowledge; c1 is high because the item is counterintuitive (the C26 floor), and since the schema's riskReason list has no counterintuitive value it carries checker_doubt. I used no WebSearch. Rival test: argued for 'false': most players assume no 19th-century composer was ever recorded; Brahms was recorded in 1889 and copies of the cylinder survive, so the statement is true. Volatility: evergreen; no time words, and nothing depends on knowledge newer than mid-2026. Regional: Brahms is known worldwide, and the surprise is the same everywhere. Style: Oxford spelling, straight quotes, no en or em dashes, explanation within 35 words. Myths: screened against myths.json, no hit. Mystery: not applicable to a practice item. Encore: not applicable to a practice item. Doubts: The original cylinder was damaged and the sound survives mainly through later copies, which is why the statement says 'there is a recording' and the explanation describes the sound, not the object.
